# stepFMR

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/jacksonmitch/stepFMR/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jacksonmitch/stepFMR/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

Finite Mixture Regression models allow relationships between the response ($\mathbf{Y}$) and the covariates $(\mathbf{X}_1,\dots, \mathbf{X}_p)$ to differ between a finite number of subpopulations. The R package, stepFMR implements stepwise procedures that select covariates having an effect on the response and determines whether each of the selected covariates has homogeneous or heterogeneous effects. The stepwise procedures are based on hypothesis testing where a weighted significance test (WEST) is used. In mixture regression, 
the unknown number of the subpopulations $G$ called the order of the mixture, poses challenges in testing the association between a covariate and the 
response. With WEST, the significance of a covariate's effects on $Y$ is the weighted sum of the significance level of all candidate $G$'s. The package supports the Gaussian, Poisson, and Binomial distribution families, and returns the effect types of each covariate, estimate of their effects, as well as the best-fitting $G$.

## Installation

You can install the development version of stepFMR from
[GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("jacksonmitch/stepFMR")
```

## Example

This example simulates data from a two-component mixture, and this known simulation
model is referred to as the true model. The stepwise procedure is performed, and then
a final model is fit with a specified structure. The vignette (`vignette("stepFMR")`) 
explains each step in more detail.

### 1. Data generation

`simulate_fmr()` generates data from a user-specified mixture regression simulation model.
This allows users to fit simulated data using the `stepFMR()` function, and compare the 
fitted results with the underlying true model. Each row of `betas` holds the regression 
coefficients of one component, with columns for the intercept and followed by the coefficients 
of the covariates. Suppose `x1` has heterogeneous effects, `x2` has homogeneous effects, 
and `x3` has no effect, with their coefficients specified in the `betas`. 
`pi` is the mixing  proportions of each component and `sigma` is the group 
specific standard deviation (only required for Gaussian mixture regression).

```{r simulate}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(stepFMR))

betas <- rbind(
  c(-2, -3, 1, 0),
  c(2, 3, 1, 0)
)
colnames(betas) <- c("(Intercept)", "x1", "x2", "x3")

sim <- simulate_fmr(
  n = 1000, betas = betas, pi = c(0.3, 0.7), sigma = c(0.5, 0.25),
  family = "gaussian", seed = 1
)
```

The simulated data in the object `sim` is a list. `sim$data` is a data frame with 
the response `y` and the covariates `x1`, `x2` and `x3`. `sim$formula` is the model formula
`y ~ x1 + x2 + x3`, which names the response on the left and the covariates on
the right, just as in `lm()` or `glm()`. `sim$true_group` records which component each
observation came from. With your own data, pass your own formula and data frame
instead, for example `stepFMR(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = my_data)`.

### 2. WEST procedure

Without specifying the order of the mixture regression model, the WEST procedure combines
statistical evidence of the association between the response and a covariate from mixture
regression models with orders ranging from 2 to `G_max`, where `G_max` can be specified 
by the user. The WEST is used in both variable selection and effect-type determination
procedures. Unless otherwise specified, by default, `stepFMR()` first performs variable 
selection and then carries out the effect-type determination procedure. Upon completion of
these procedures, the model order is selected from the range of 2 to `G_max` based on the 
lowest BIC value. In this example `G_max` = 3, therefore the model order is selected from
orders 2 and 3.

```{r west}
fit <- stepFMR(sim$formula, sim$data, G_max = 3)
print(fit)
```

The printed result in `fit` lists the selected covariates, the effect type of each
selected covariate, and the selected order of the final model. `print_steps()` 
shows the weighted p-value of every candidate at each step. In each step of the forward 
variable selection procedure, a candidate variable is added when its p-value is the smallest
and below `alpha` (0.05 by default). In the forward effect-type procedure, if a candidate 
variable has the smallest p-value and that p-value is below `alpha`, its effect-type is 
set to heterogeneous.

```{r steps}
print_steps(fit$variable_selection)
print_steps(fit$effect_determination)
```

### 3. Fitting

If the effect types of all covariates in a given set of covariates are specified,
`fitFMR()` fits the model without going through the stepwise procedures. Here the
covariates are the ones selected above, `x1` and `x2`. `common = "x2"`
sets the effect type of `x2` to homogeneous, and covariates not in `common` all have
heterogeneous effects by default. `G` specifies the candidate orders to fit, here 2 and 3,
and the final model is the one with the lowest BIC.


```{r fit}
fit_fixed <- fitFMR(y ~ x1 + x2, sim$data, G = 2:3, common = "x2")
fit_fixed
```

Mixture components have no natural order, so the fitted components can be
numbered differently from the simulated ones. In a simulation study, the true grouping
information is known. `match_groups()` relabels the fitted groups that best align with
the true underlying groups such that the regression parameters can be compared directly
with the `betas` specified in the simulation model. 

```{r match}
aligned <- match_groups(fit, sim$true_group)
aligned$best_fit$parameter_values[["beta_g"]]
```

### Other families

The package supports `family = "poisson"` and `family = "binomial"`. For binomial data
the response is `cbind(successes, failures)`, the number of trials for each observation
is specified by `size`.

```{r poisson}
sim_pois <- simulate_fmr(
  n = 500,
  betas = rbind(c(-0.5, -1, 0.3, 0), c(0.5, 1, 0.3, 0)),
  pi = c(0.4, 0.6), family = "poisson", seed = 2
)
fit_pois <- stepFMR(sim_pois$formula, sim_pois$data, G_max = 3, family = "poisson")
print(fit_pois)
```

```{r binomial}
sim_bin <- simulate_fmr(
  n = 500,
  betas = rbind(c(-1, -3, 0.5, 0), c(1, 3, 0.5, 0)),
  pi = c(0.4, 0.6), family = "binomial", size = 25, seed = 3
)
fit_bin <- stepFMR(sim_bin$formula, sim_bin$data, G_max = 3, family = "binomial")
print(fit_bin)
```

## Reference

Gan, C., Chen, J. and Feng, Z. (2024). Tests of covariate effects under finite Gaussian mixture regression models. *Journal of Applied Statistics*, 52(8), 1571-1593. <https://doi.org/10.1080/02664763.2024.2433567>
